content: Poison sumac, scientifically known as Toxicodendron vernix or Rhus vernix, is a woody shrub or small tree that can grow up to 7 meters (approximately 20 feet) in height. Every part of this plant contains a resin called urushiol, which is highly irritating to human skin and mucous membranes. When the plant is burned, inhaling the smoke can lead to internal irritations, including diarrhea. Description of the Plant The tree has a rounded and narrow crown, with slender, pendulous branches. It often appears as a shrub rather than a full tree. The leaves are compound and pinnate, measuring 25–50 cm in length, and consist of 7 to 13 leaflets. Each leaflet is 4–10 cm long and can sometimes be mistaken for individual leaves. The veins from which the leaflets grow are distinctly red. The plant produces small, white or gray berries in panicles that are 10–20 cm long. These berries are a key distinguishing feature, as other sumac species typically have red berries. Poison sumac also differs from other sumacs by having shorter leaves, fewer leaflets, and leaf margins that are smooth (entire). It thrives in wet soils, such as swamps and peat bogs, unlike other sumacs that prefer dry environments. Bark: The bark is smooth and can range from light to dark gray, with slight striations. Branchlets: These are smooth and reddish-brown, covered with small, orange-colored lenticular spots. Over time, they transition to orange-brown and eventually light gray. Wood: The wood is light yellow with brown streaks, soft, coarse-grained, and brittle. Its specific gravity is approximately 0.4382, and a cubic foot weighs about 27–31 pounds. Winter Buds: The terminal bud is significantly larger than the axillary buds. All buds are acute and dark purple in color. Leaves: The leaves are alternate and pinnately compound, measuring 7–14 inches in length. They are borne on slender, reddish petioles. The leaflets, numbering 7 to 13, are obovate or oblong, 3–4 inches long, and slightly unequal at the base. The apex of the leaflets is either acute or rounded. The terminal leaflet sometimes has a stalk about an inch long. When emerging from the bud, the leaves are orange and downy. Once mature, they are smooth, dark green, and shiny on the upper surface, while pale beneath. The midrib and primary veins are prominent. In autumn, the leaves turn vibrant shades of scarlet and orange. Flowers: Poison sumac flowers in June and July. The plant is dioecious, meaning male and female flowers are borne on separate plants. The flowers are yellow-green and grow in long, narrow, axillary panicles near the ends of the branches. The bracts and bractlets are acute, downy, and fall off as the flowers open. Calyx: The calyx is five-lobed, with short, acute lobes. Corolla: The corolla consists of five acute, yellow-green petals. Stamens: There are five stamens with long, slender filaments and large, orange-colored anthers. In fertile flowers, the stamens are short and rudimentary. Pistil: The ovary is ovoid-globose, one-celled, and topped with three thick, spreading styles. It contains a solitary ovule. Fruit: The fruit is a drupaceous, globular, white berry that grows in long, graceful racemes. The berries are often tipped with the dark remnants of the styles. They ripen in September and frequently remain on the tree throughout the winter. The cotyledons are flat and leaf-like. Distribution Poison sumac is found exclusively in very wet or flooded soils, such as swamps and peat bogs. Its range includes the eastern United States and Canada. In the United States, it can grow as far west as southern Idaho. Toxicity In the United States, poison sumac is classified as a noxious weed under the Federal Noxious Weed Act of 1974. Many states also categorize it similarly. It is considered one of the most invasive weed species in the U.S. Poison sumac is significantly more virulent in causing urushiol-induced contact dermatitis than its relatives, poison ivy and poison oak. Some botanists regard poison sumac as the most toxic plant species in the United States. Avoidance, Treatment, and Safety For detailed information on preventing and treating rashes caused by urushiol, refer to resources on urushiol-induced contact dermatitis.
